# Turkish and Morphologically Rich Languages {#sec-turkish-nlp}

::: {.callout-note appearance="simple" icon="false"}
**Chapter status: drafted.** The measurements new to this chapter were run on
the WMT16/17/18 Turkish–English test sets — 9,007 professionally translated
sentence pairs, which give the same content in two languages and so allow
comparisons the usual monolingual corpora cannot. Where a number was measured
in an earlier chapter it is cited rather than repeated. Software:
`sacrebleu` 2.6.0, `snowballstemmer` 3.1.1, `transformers` 5.15.1, PyTorch
2.13.0 on Python 3.14.5.
:::

**Learning objectives.** After this chapter you can:

- explain what agglutination does to vocabulary size, and show the effect on
  a corpus rather than asserting it;
- predict which parts of an NLP pipeline a morphologically rich language will
  break, and check them in the right order;
- normalize Turkish text without destroying it, and name the two bugs that
  survive every code review;
- decide between a multilingual and a monolingual model from a measurement
  rather than a preference;
- recognise the general pattern this book has hit repeatedly: a standard tool
  that is silently wrong outside English, and the kind of control that catches
  it.

## What agglutination actually costs {#sec-turkish-nlp-agglutination}

Turkish builds words by stacking suffixes onto a stem, each one adding a
piece of grammar, in an order fixed by rule and with vowels that harmonise
with the stem. *Ev* is house; *evler* houses; *evlerimiz* our houses;
*evlerimizden* from our houses. English needs four words for the last one.

Everyone knows this. What it *costs* is rarely measured, and the measurement
needs a corpus where both languages say the same thing — which is exactly
what a professional translation is.

### Vocabulary growth, on identical content

```text
WMT16/17/18 tr-en, 9,007 aligned sentence pairs

  Turkish   141,412 tokens   32,866 distinct forms
  English   182,429 tokens   16,652 distinct forms
```

[Turkish produces twice the vocabulary from 78% of the tokens.]{.hl} Same
content, same facts, same news stories. And the ratio is not fixed — it grows
with the corpus:

```text
   tokens seen     TR forms    EN forms    ratio
         5,000        2,471       1,655     1.49
        10,000        4,192       2,575     1.63
        25,000        9,342       5,016     1.86
        50,000       15,963       7,827     2.04
       100,000       25,664      11,848     2.17
       141,412       32,866      14,251     2.31
```

That widening is the important part. English vocabulary growth flattens as
the common words get used up; **Turkish keeps producing forms it has not used
before**, because the forms are generated by rule rather than drawn from a
list. A vocabulary is a list, and productive morphology does not fit in one.

The tail shows the same thing:

```text
  forms occurring exactly once     Turkish   58.6%      English   44.1%
```

::: {.column-margin}
@sec-bake-off measured 58.6% hapax on a completely different Turkish corpus —
product reviews rather than news. Two unrelated corpora landing on the same
figure is a coincidence in the third digit, but the agreement in the first two
is not: it is what a productive morphology does to any Turkish text you pick.
:::

### One stem, many words

Stemming the same corpus and counting the surface forms each stem produced:

```text
  32,866 distinct forms  ->  17,891 stems       mean 1.84 forms per stem

  arkadaş   39 forms   arkadaş, arkadaşı, arkadaşım, arkadaşın, arkadaştı, ...
  ülke      35 forms   ülke, ülkem, ülkede, ülkeyi, ülkeye, ülkeden, ülkeler, ...
  el        34 forms   el, eli, ele, elim, elde, elin, elimi, ...
  çocuk     31 forms   çocuk, çocuğu, çocuğa, çocukla, çocuğun, çocukta, ...
```

The mean of 1.84 is misleading downward — 75% of stems appear only once in a
corpus this small, and the stemmer under-merges. The informative row is the
top: **thirty-nine forms of one everyday noun in 141,000 tokens**, and the
list is nowhere near exhausted. @sec-bake-off, on a larger corpus, found 895
forms sharing the stem *kulla*.

### Where this shows up

Agglutination is not one problem; it is the same problem arriving in five
places, each of which this book has now measured:

| where | what happens | measured in |
|:--|:--|:--|
| Tokenization | more tokens per word, so more cost and less effective context | @sec-pretraining |
| Vocabulary | twice the types, a longer tail, more out-of-vocabulary | here |
| Lexical retrieval | a query form that differs from the document form matches nothing | @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval |
| Word-level metrics | fewer tokens per sentence, so each error costs more | @sec-machine-translation |
| Case folding | one character breaks the whole pipeline | @sec-turkish-nlp-normalization |

: One property, five consequences {tbl-colwidths="[22,52,26]"}

## Turkish normalization, and the two bugs that survive review {#sec-turkish-nlp-normalization}

Normalization in English is a preprocessing decision. In Turkish two of its
steps are correctness bugs, and both are invisible in code review because the
code looks right.

### Bug one: `str.lower()` is wrong in both directions

Turkish has two letters where English has one. Dotted `İ`/`i` and dotless
`I`/`ı` are different letters with different sounds, and the case mapping
between them is not the ASCII one:

```text
        English rules          Turkish rules
  I  →  i                      ı
  İ  →  i + combining dot      i
```

Every mainstream `lower()` applies the English rules unless told otherwise.
On the WMT16 Turkish source:

```text
  words containing I or İ                                    438
  where str.lower() differs from Turkish lowercasing         438   (100%)

    'İtiraf'      str.lower() 'i̇tiraf'       Turkish 'itiraf'
    'İngilizce'   str.lower() 'i̇ngilizce'    Turkish 'ingilizce'
    'İşlerin'     str.lower() 'i̇şlerin'      Turkish 'işlerin'
```

**Every single one.** Not a long tail — a total failure on any word beginning
with a capital dotted İ, which in Turkish includes a large share of proper
nouns and every sentence-initial word starting with *i*.

### Bug two: the result is not even one word any more

The first bug is a wrong string. The second is worse, and it is the one
@sec-clustering found in production:

```text
  'İSTANBUL'.lower()  =  'i̇stanbul'

    code points  U+0069 U+0307 U+0073 U+0074 U+0061 U+006E U+0062 U+0075 U+006C
                   i     ̇      s      t      a      n      b      u      l
    categories   Ll     Mn     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll     Ll

  re.findall(r"\w+", 'İSTANBUL'.lower())   →   ['i', 'stanbul']
```

`U+0307 COMBINING DOT ABOVE` is a *nonspacing mark*, not a word character.
Every tokenizer built on `\w+` therefore splits the word in two at that point.
[`İstanbul` becomes `i` plus `stanbul`, and no amount of downstream modelling
recovers from it]{.hl} — the model never sees the word.

And it does not go away when you normalize:

```text
  unicodedata.normalize("NFC",  'İSTANBUL'.lower())   →   ['i', 'stanbul']
  'TAVSİYE'.lower()                                   →   ['tavsi', 'ye']
```

NFC does not recombine, because `i` + combining dot is not canonically
equivalent to `i` — the composed character `i̇` does not exist as a single code
point. There is no Unicode-level fix. The fix is to not create the problem:

```python
def tr_lower(s):
    return s.replace("İ", "i").replace("I", "ı").lower()

def tr_upper(s):
    return s.replace("i", "İ").replace("ı", "I").upper()
```

Four lines, applied before anything else touches the text.

::: {.column-margin}
This is why the bug survives: the code that causes it is `text.lower()`, which
is correct-looking, ubiquitous, and inside every library you did not write.
@sec-clustering found it because a cluster came back 94.7% full of one
artefact — not because anyone was looking for it. Check for it by lowercasing
a word with `İ` and printing the code points.
:::

### Diacritics: deasciification and what it merges

Turkish keyboards are not universal, and a large amount of real Turkish is
written without diacritics — *guzel* for *güzel*, *cok* for *çok*. Handling it
means either restoring the diacritics (deasciification) or stripping them
everywhere so both forms match.

Stripping is the tempting one-liner. Measured on the same corpus:

```text
  words containing a Turkish-specific character   19,318 / 46,243   (41.8%)
  distinct forms                                          15,173
  distinct forms after stripping diacritics               15,101
  ascii forms now ambiguous between 2+ real words             72

     'oldu'   <-  oldu, öldü          (it happened / he died)
     'bas'    <-  bas, baş            (press / head)
     'once'   <-  once, önce          (once / before)
     'mi'     <-  mi, mı              (two different question particles)
```

Only 72 collisions, which sounds harmless until you read them. *Oldu* and
*öldü* are "it happened" and "he died". [The merge rate is low and the cost
per merge is total]{.hl}, which is the worst shape a preprocessing decision
can have: it will not show up in aggregate metrics and it will produce
individually catastrophic errors.

Restore rather than strip, if you can afford it. If you must strip, strip the
*query* and the *document* both, and know that you have made those pairs
indistinguishable.

## Morphological analysis, and whether you still need it {#sec-turkish-nlp-analysis}

Before subword tokenizers, handling Turkish meant *analysing* it: taking
*evlerimizden* and returning the stem *ev* plus an ordered list of the
grammatical functions stacked on it. Turkish has one of the field's great
success stories here — @oflazer1994two built a two-level finite-state
analyser that covers the language's morphology properly, and its descendants
still work.

Two things make analysis harder than it sounds:

**Ambiguity.** *Yüzü* can be *his face*, *the swimmer*, or *a hundred of it*,
depending on which analysis you take. A morphological analyser returns all of
them; picking the right one is *morphological disambiguation*, and it needs
sentence context. So the tidy pipeline — analyse, then model — has a
sentence-level model inside its first step.

**Coverage.** An analyser knows the stems it was built with. New words,
brand names, and the productive compounding that Turkish does freely fall
outside it, and the failure mode is a hard one: no analysis at all.

### So do you need it in 2026?

For most modelling, no. Subword tokenization (@sec-text-as-data) handles
morphology *statistically* rather than linguistically: it does not know that
*-lerimizden* is four suffixes, but it learns that the piece recurs, which is
most of what a model needs. That is why BERTurk works without a morphological
analyser anywhere in the stack.

Reach for a real analyser when you need something a subword model does not
give you:

- **Lexical retrieval**, where you need the stem to index on —
  @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval measures exactly how much this is worth.
- **Linguistic annotation**, where the grammatical analysis *is* the output.
- **Rule-driven products** — grammar checkers, spelling correction,
  dictionary lookup — where a wrong answer must be explainable.
- **Very low data regimes**, where the inductive bias of knowing that
  *evlerimizden* and *evimiz* share a stem is worth more than the data you do
  not have.

::: {.column-margin}
The compromise most projects land on is a stemmer rather than an analyser:
crude, fast, no ambiguity to resolve, and — as @sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval
shows — carrying most of the benefit for retrieval. The Snowball Turkish
stemmer used throughout this chapter is a hundred lines of rules. It
under-merges, it over-merges, and it takes recall@1 from 28.0% to 95.3%.
:::

## Turkish retrieval: how much of the gap is morphology {#sec-turkish-nlp-retrieval}

Search in Turkish is harder than search in English, and practitioners
generally know it. What is worth knowing is *how much* of the difficulty is
morphology alone — because that part has a cheap fix, and the rest does not.

The experiment isolates it. Take 7,165 Turkish sentences as documents, index
them with BM25, and query with three content words drawn from a target
document — but in a **different surface form than the document uses**. That is
the real case: the user types *İstanbul*, the document says *İstanbul'da*.

```text
7,165 Turkish documents (sentences of 8+ words)
1,481 queries of 3 terms each
69% of query terms are a different inflection than the document uses

index / query scheme      recall@1   recall@10   terms/doc
surface form                 28.0%       54.4%        15.7
5-char prefix                74.6%       92.6%        15.7
Snowball stem                95.3%       99.8%        15.7
character 4-grams            74.9%       94.9%        55.7
```

[Surface-form BM25 finds the right document 28% of the time. Stemming takes
it to 95.3%.]{.hl} One preprocessing step, a 3.4× improvement, and no model
involved at all.

Read the setup before you take the headline anywhere: 69% of query terms were
deliberately chosen to be a different inflection, and a query only succeeds if
enough of its three terms match. That is harsher than an average query and
gentler than the worst one — a user searching a Turkish corpus types the
dictionary form, and the corpus almost never contains it.

Three practical consequences:

1. **Stemming is not optional in Turkish lexical search.** In English it is a
   marginal tweak worth a point or two. Here it is the difference between a
   search box that works and one that does not.
2. **Character n-grams are the robust fallback.** 74.9% recall@1 with no
   linguistic knowledge at all, at the cost of 3.5× the index size (55.7
   terms per document against 15.7). When you have no stemmer for a language,
   this is the move.
3. **Prefix truncation is a surprisingly good approximation.** Keeping the
   first five characters gets 74.6% — nearly the same as character n-grams, at
   no index cost. It is crude, it is wrong on short words, and it is what to
   reach for when a real stemmer is not available.

::: {.column-margin}
This is also the strongest single argument for dense retrieval in Turkish:
an embedding of *İstanbul'da* and an embedding of *İstanbul* are close
whatever the tokenizer did, because the model learned them from context rather
than matching strings. @sec-retrieval builds that properly. The measurement
here is what the sparse half of a hybrid retriever needs in order to pull its
weight — and untreated, it does not.
:::

## The five-chapter pattern {#sec-turkish-nlp-pattern}

Something has happened repeatedly in this book, and it is worth naming as a
pattern rather than leaving as a handful of anecdotes. In each case a standard,
widely-used tool produced a number that was silently wrong on Turkish, and in
each case a *control measurement* — not a better model — is what exposed it.

| chapter | the tool | what it did on Turkish | how it surfaced |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| @sec-bake-off | `str.lower()` | `IYI` → `iyi` under English rules, `ıyı` under Turkish | comparing the two case mappings side by side |
| @sec-clustering | `str.lower()` | `İ` becomes `i` + a combining mark, splitting the word | a cluster that was 94.7% one artefact |
| @sec-sequence-labeling | WikiANN | 13.06% of the test set sitting verbatim in training | hashing test inputs against training inputs |
| @sec-summarization | `rouge-score` | 44.4% of Turkish words mutilated by its tokenizer | two implementations of one metric disagreeing |
| @sec-summarization | a faithfulness proxy | reported human journalists as 56% unfaithful | scoring copied text, which cannot be unfaithful |
| @sec-machine-translation | BLEU | 29% fewer tokens per sentence, so each error costs more | the same semantic error, run in two languages |

: Six silent failures, and the control that caught each {tbl-colwidths="[20,14,38,28]"}

Three things generalise, and none of them is about Turkish specifically.

**The tools were not broken; they were untested outside their assumptions.**
`rouge-score` reproduces the original Perl behaviour faithfully. BLEU does
exactly what its definition says. WikiANN was built as described. Each is
correct on the language it was validated on, and each carries an assumption
its documentation does not state.

**Every one was caught by a control, not by inspection.** Copied text that
must score perfectly; a majority-class floor; the same error in two languages;
test inputs hashed against training. [When you cannot verify a metric
directly, feed it an input whose correct answer you already know.]{.hl} That
habit found every one of them, and reading the code found none.

**The failures were silent by construction.** No exception, no warning, no
missing field — just a number that was 60% too high, or a benchmark that was
13% memorisation. A pipeline that fails loudly is a pipeline you will fix. The
ones to worry about are the ones that return a plausible float.

::: {.column-margin}
If you work in a language that is not English, expect this and budget for it.
The practical version: before trusting any tool on your language, run it on an
input whose answer is known — identical strings, empty strings, a copied
document, a single-token change — and check that the number is what it must be.
Ten minutes, and it is the highest-return ten minutes in a non-English NLP
project.
:::

## Turkish corpora, models, and benchmarks {#sec-turkish-nlp-ecosystem}

::: {.callout-warning appearance="simple"}
This section dates faster than anything else in the book. Treat the names as a
map of *kinds* of resource rather than a leaderboard, and check what is
current before committing to one.
:::

**Encoders.** BERTurk [@schweter2020berturk] remains the default Turkish
encoder and is what @sec-sequence-labeling and @sec-classification fine-tuned.
It exists in cased and uncased variants, and for Turkish the **cased** one is
almost always right — see @sec-turkish-nlp-normalization for what the uncasing
step does to `İ`.

**Multilingual encoders.** mBERT and XLM-R [@conneau2020unsupervised] cover
Turkish among a hundred other languages. @sec-turkish-nlp-decide measures what
that costs.

**Generative models.** The Turkish-specific generative landscape — TURNA,
Kanarya, Trendyol's and Cosmos's LLMs, and the Turkish-adapted Llama and
Qwen derivatives — changes every few months. What does not change is the
question to ask about each: *what was it trained on, and can you use it?*
Licence terms on regionally-released models vary far more than on the big
international releases, and a model you cannot deploy commercially is not a
candidate.

**Benchmarks.** Mukayese [@safaya2022mukayese] assembled Turkish baselines
across tasks precisely because the field kept reporting Turkish numbers that
could not be compared with each other. Turkish versions of the standard
suites — question answering, multi-task knowledge — exist and are used.

Two cautions about all of them, both of which this book has already
demonstrated on other corpora:

1. **Translation artefacts.** A benchmark translated from English tests
   translated-English competence, not Turkish. Translationese has different
   word order, different sentence length, and vocabulary chosen by a
   translation system. Check whether the benchmark was written in Turkish or
   rendered into it.
2. **Contamination.** @sec-sequence-labeling found 13.06% of a standard
   Turkish NER benchmark's test set sitting verbatim in its own training set —
   in a resource used by hundreds of papers. Hash your test inputs against
   training before you believe a score, and against the model's pretraining
   corpus if you can.

## Multilingual or monolingual: deciding with a measurement {#sec-turkish-nlp-decide}

The question arrives on every Turkish project, and it is usually answered by
preference. Here it is answered by running both.

`bert-base-multilingual-cased` and `dbmdz/bert-base-turkish-cased` are
comparable models — same architecture, same era, same fine-tuning recipe —
differing in what they were pretrained on. @sec-sequence-labeling's NER setup,
identical in every other respect, gives the comparison.

```text
WikiANN Turkish NER, 20,000 training sentences, identical recipe

model                     span P  span R  span F1   macro   train s   infer s
BERTurk (monolingual)      91.49   92.35    91.92   91.82     476.6      10.3
mBERT  (multilingual)      92.25   93.27    92.76   92.67     537.5       8.8
```

**The multilingual model won, by 0.84 span F1.** That is the opposite of what
this section was set up to show, and it is worth working through rather than
explaining away.

### First, the comparison is fairer than it looks

The obvious objection is size — mBERT has 177.3M parameters against BERTurk's
110.0M. But look at where the difference is:

```text
model                    total    embeddings   transformer body
BERTurk                 110.0M         24.6M              85.5M
mBERT                   177.3M         91.8M              85.5M
```

[The transformer bodies are identical.]{.hl} Twelve layers, same width, same
85.5M parameters doing the actual computation. The entire difference is the
embedding table, which is a lookup indexed by vocabulary size — 32,000 entries
against 119,547. mBERT is not a bigger *model*; it is the same model carrying
a larger dictionary.

And it wins **despite** a worse tokenizer for Turkish, measured on the same
test set:

```text
model                     vocab    subwords/word   mean sequence length
BERTurk                  32,000             1.66                   14.5
mBERT                   119,547             1.97                   16.8
```

mBERT spends 19% more tokens on the same Turkish text, with a vocabulary 3.7×
larger — because most of that vocabulary belongs to other languages.

### Second, the confound that most likely explains it

**WikiANN is built from Wikipedia. mBERT was pretrained on Wikipedia.**

That is not a small coincidence; it is a domain match between the benchmark
and one model's pretraining corpus, and it is the most plausible reason for
the result. BERTurk was trained on a broader Turkish mix, so on this
particular corpus it is the one working out of domain.

[The honest reading is therefore not "multilingual models are better for
Turkish".]{.hl} It is: *on a Wikipedia-derived task, the model pretrained on
Wikipedia won by 0.84 points, despite tokenizing the language worse.*

### So what this section actually gives you is a protocol

There is no general verdict here, and anyone offering one is selling
something. What there is, is a decision procedure — four measurements, in
this order, because the cheap ones often decide it before the expensive one
runs:

1. **Fertility on *your* text.** Tokens per word for each candidate, on your
   own domain. Convert to cost and to effective context length
   (@sec-pretraining). This is an hour's work and it sometimes ends the
   discussion.
2. **Domain overlap.** What was each model pretrained on, and how close is it
   to your data? The measurement above is mostly a demonstration of how much
   this matters.
3. **The task itself, both models, identical recipe.** Same data, same
   hyper-parameters, same seed. Anything else is not a comparison.
4. **The operational columns.** Training time, inference latency, memory. Here
   mBERT trained 13% slower and — despite longer sequences — ran inference
   slightly faster, which is a reminder to measure rather than reason about
   throughput.

@rust2021good is the systematic version of this question: how much of the
monolingual advantage is the tokenizer rather than the model. Their answer,
across languages, is *a lot of it* — which makes step 1 the right place to
start.

::: {.column-margin}
Note what the result does *not* undermine. mBERT still fragments Turkish 19%
worse, which is a permanent tax on cost and context that no accuracy number
removes. If this task had been a generation task billed per token rather than
a tagging task scored per span, the same two models would produce a different
verdict from the same measurements.
:::

## Intuition checks {#sec-turkish-nlp-intuition}

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 1. Your Turkish search box returns nothing useful. Where do you look first?

Not the ranker, and not the embeddings. Look at whether you are indexing
surface forms.

Measured on 7,165 Turkish documents with queries whose terms are inflected
differently from the documents: surface-form BM25 gets **28.0%** recall@1,
Snowball stemming gets **95.3%**. A user types the dictionary form; the corpus
contains an inflected one; exact string matching finds nothing.

If you have no Turkish stemmer, character 4-grams get 74.9% at 3.5× the index
size, and truncating to five characters gets 74.6% for free.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 2. Why is `text.lower()` a correctness bug rather than a style choice?

Two reasons, and the second is worse.

Turkish has four letters where English has two — `İ i I ı` — and the case
mapping is not the ASCII one. On the WMT16 Turkish source, **438 of 438**
words containing `I` or `İ` come out differently under English rules.

Then: `'İSTANBUL'.lower()` produces `i` followed by `U+0307 COMBINING DOT
ABOVE`, which is a nonspacing mark and not a word character. So
`re.findall(r"\w+", ...)` returns `['i', 'stanbul']` — the word is split in
two, and NFC normalization does not put it back. The model never sees
`istanbul` at all.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 3. Should you strip Turkish diacritics so `guzel` matches `güzel`?

Only with your eyes open. On the WMT16 source it merges 15,173 forms into
15,101 — just **72 collisions** — which looks like a free win until you read
them: *oldu* / *öldü* is "it happened" / "he died". *bas* / *baş* is "press" /
"head".

The shape of that trade is the worst one available: too rare to show up in an
aggregate metric, and catastrophic in each individual case. Restore the
diacritics if you can afford it. If you must strip, strip both sides and
document that those pairs are now indistinguishable.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 4. How much bigger is a Turkish vocabulary, really?

On identical content — 9,007 professionally translated sentence pairs —
Turkish produced **32,866 distinct forms from 141,412 tokens** against
English's **16,652 from 182,429**. Twice the vocabulary from 78% of the
tokens.

The number that matters more is that the ratio *grows*: 1.49 at 5,000 tokens,
2.31 at 141,000. English vocabulary saturates; Turkish keeps generating forms
by rule. Any design that assumes a vocabulary can be enumerated — a fixed word
list, a closed feature set, an exact-match index — is fighting that.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 5. A colleague reports a Turkish benchmark score of 85. What do you ask?

Three questions, in order.

**Was the benchmark written in Turkish or translated into it?** A translated
benchmark measures competence on translationese.

**Is the test set in the training set?** @sec-sequence-labeling found 13.06%
of a widely-used Turkish NER benchmark's test set verbatim in its own
training split. Hashing takes four lines.

**What did the tokenizer do?** @sec-summarization found the standard ROUGE
implementation mutilating 44.4% of Turkish words. If the score came out of a
tool that was validated on English, the score is a hypothesis.
:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## 6. When is a multilingual model the right choice for Turkish?

When you need one deployment for many languages, when you need cross-lingual
transfer from a language with more labelled data, or when no monolingual model
exists for your language.

What you give up is measurable rather than mysterious: a multilingual
tokenizer spends more tokens per Turkish word, which costs money and context
(@sec-pretraining), and it spends vocabulary on languages you are not using.

But do not assume the accuracy follows. @sec-turkish-nlp-decide ran both on
the same task and **the multilingual model won by 0.84 span F1**, despite
needing 19% more tokens for the same text — because the benchmark's domain
matched its pretraining corpus. Measure fertility first, domain second, and
the task third.
:::

## Lab: a Turkish evaluation suite you can trust {#sec-turkish-nlp-lab}

The point of this lab is not to rank models. It is to build an evaluation you
would defend, on a language the tools were not validated on.

### Step 1 — write three tasks, in Turkish, yourself

Fifty items each. Classification, extraction, and something generative. Write
them in Turkish rather than translating from English, because a translated
suite measures translationese. Keep them boring and unambiguous — you are
building a measuring instrument, not a challenge set.

### Step 2 — validate the scorer before scoring anything

Feed each metric a **perfect prediction** and confirm it returns a perfect
score. Then feed it a copied input, an empty prediction, and a prediction that
differs by one character. Write down what each *should* return before you run
it.

This step is the whole lab. @sec-summarization found a standard metric
mutilating 44.4% of Turkish words; it was caught exactly this way and by
nothing else.

### Step 3 — check your own text for the two normalization bugs

Lowercase your suite and search for `U+0307`. Count words containing `İ` and
compare `str.lower()` against `tr_lower()` on each. If your suite already
contains the bug, every model you evaluate will be scored on damaged input.

### Step 4 — measure fertility and convert it to money

For each model you plan to test, tokens per Turkish word on your own text.
Multiply by your request volume. This number often decides the choice before
accuracy does.

### Step 5 — run three models, including one multilingual

A Turkish-specific model, a multilingual one, and an LLM. Report accuracy,
tokens per request, latency, and cost per thousand requests — four columns,
because the first one alone has never decided a deployment.

### Step 6 — audit for contamination

Hash your suite's items against anything you know about the models' training
data. You will usually not be able to check a pretraining corpus; say so
explicitly rather than leaving it implied.

### What to hand in

The four-column table, the scorer-validation log from step 2 with its
predicted-versus-actual column, and a paragraph naming which model you would
ship and what would change your mind.

## What to remember {#sec-turkish-nlp-summary}

- **Agglutination is measurable, and it compounds.** On identical content,
  Turkish produced **32,866 distinct forms from 141,412 tokens** against
  English's **16,652 from 182,429** — twice the vocabulary from 78% of the
  tokens. The ratio grows with corpus size (1.49 → 2.31), because Turkish
  generates forms by rule rather than drawing them from a list. Any design
  that assumes a vocabulary can be enumerated is fighting that.

- **`str.lower()` is a correctness bug in Turkish, twice over.** All **438 of
  438** words containing `I` or `İ` in the WMT16 source come out wrong under
  English rules. And `'İSTANBUL'.lower()` emits `i` plus a combining mark, so
  `\w+` returns `['i', 'stanbul']` — the word splits and NFC does not repair
  it. Four lines of `tr_lower` before anything else touches the text.

- **Stemming is not optional in Turkish lexical search.** Surface-form BM25:
  **28.0%** recall@1. Snowball stemming: **95.3%**. Character 4-grams get
  74.9% with no linguistic knowledge, at 3.5× the index. In English this is a
  tweak; here it is whether the search box works.

- **Stripping diacritics merges 72 forms and each merge is total.** *oldu* and
  *öldü* — "it happened" and "he died" — become the same string. Rare enough
  to pass every aggregate metric, severe enough to matter every time.

- **A multilingual model beat the monolingual one on this task**, 92.76
  against 91.92 span F1 — with identical transformer bodies (85.5M each; the
  parameter gap is all embedding table) and *despite* tokenizing Turkish 19%
  worse. The likely reason is domain: the benchmark is built from Wikipedia
  and mBERT was pretrained on Wikipedia. There is no general verdict here,
  only a protocol — fertility on your text, domain overlap, both models on
  your task with an identical recipe, then the operational columns.

- **Subword tokenization replaced morphological analysis for modelling, not
  for everything.** Reach for a real analyser when the grammar is the output,
  when a wrong answer must be explainable, or when you need the stem to index
  on — and note that a hundred-line stemmer carried most of the retrieval
  benefit.

- **The pattern, across five chapters: standard tools fail silently outside
  English.** `str.lower()`, `rouge-score`, BLEU, a benchmark's own splits, and
  a faithfulness proxy written for this book each produced a plausible wrong
  number on Turkish. None raised an error. Every one was caught by a **control
  measurement** — an input whose correct answer was known in advance — and none
  by reading the code. The last entry on that list is ours, which is the point:
  the failure mode is not other people's carelessness.

- **So build the control first.** Before trusting a tool on your language,
  give it something whose answer cannot be in doubt: identical strings, copied
  text, a perfect prediction, a majority-class floor. Ten minutes, and it is
  the highest-return ten minutes in a non-English NLP project.

## Exercises {#sec-turkish-nlp-exercises}

1. **Vocabulary growth in your language.** Take any professionally translated
   parallel corpus and plot distinct forms against tokens for both sides.
   Report the ratio at three corpus sizes and say whether it is widening.

2. **Break the lowercaser.** Find a Turkish word where `str.lower()` produces
   something `re.findall(r"\w+", ...)` splits in two. Print the code points.
   Then check whether the libraries in your own stack have the same problem.

3. **The retrieval fix, on your data.** Index a Turkish corpus with BM25 twice,
   surface forms and stems. Query with dictionary forms. Report recall@1 for
   both, and decide what your search box should do.

4. **The diacritic collision list.** Strip diacritics from a Turkish
   vocabulary and list every ascii form that now maps to two or more real
   words. Rank them by how badly the confusion would matter in your domain.

5. **Fertility to invoice.** Take a Turkish document and its English
   translation, tokenize both with the tokenizer your product actually uses,
   and convert the difference into a monthly bill at your request volume. Then
   do it with a Turkish-native tokenizer and report the difference
   (@sec-pretraining has the method).

6. **Audit a Turkish benchmark.** Pick one you would use. Check for
   translation artefacts, hash its test set against its training set, and run
   its scoring script on a perfect prediction to confirm it returns a perfect
   score. Report what you find, including if the answer is "nothing wrong".

7. **The control habit.** Take any metric you rely on and feed it an input
   whose correct answer you know for certain — identical strings, a copied
   document, an empty prediction. Write down what it should return and what it
   did. This exercise has a low hit rate and an enormous payoff.
